text: {"answer":"The evidence mostly suggests remote work modestly increases productivity, but the effect depends on conditions. A meta-analysis of 82 studies (3,574 estimates) finds a small but positive average effect of working from home on productivity, driven by gains in hourly productivity and more hours worked [0a130e4f39dc#0]. A review of 50+ studies reports a median impact of +10% for focused tasks but -4% for collaborative tasks [d658dc380b73#5]. Bloom's randomized trial at Trip.com found a hybrid schedule showed no measurable productivity difference from in-office peers [d658dc380b73#5]. Contradicting evidence is weaker but real: a study finds full-remote work (five days a week) was associated with reduced work productivity and increased presenteeism risk [abefd158b9c2#2]. Personality also matters, as conscientiousness predicts higher self-reported WFH productivity [44ecc13330bd#0]. Overall, remote work tends to help, especially for focused tasks, while full-time remote arrangements may hurt for some workers.","confidence":68,"one_line":"Remote work shows a small net productivity gain, strongest for focused tasks, but full-time remote may reduce output for some workers."}
